title: Training Data Attribution in Diffusion Models via Mirrored Unlearning and Noise-Consistent Skew
topic: Data-centric AI->Data-centric AI methods and tools
claim: A model retrained on much less data still generates nearly identical samples from the same seed, so outputs reveal little about which data mattered.
layout: 3 stacked dataset panels, each with Pre/Post rows of 10 paired columns
description: The figure is a gallery of generated images in three stacked blocks, labeled CIFAR10, ArtBench10 and COCO. Each block is a 2-row by 10-column grid of small square images with thick black borders. The rows are labeled Pre (original pre-trained model) and Post (model trained after 40% random data removal), written vertically on the left. Each column pairs images generated from the same seed. The Pre and Post images look almost the same in every column. Examples are airplanes, horses and trucks for CIFAR10, paintings and portraits for ArtBench10, and food, snow, towers, surfers and buses for COCO. There are no arrows, equations or method boxes. The eye goes first to the colorful image grids, then to the row-by-row comparison within each column.
caption: Examples of images generated using the original pre-trained model (Pre) and the post-trained model with 40% random data removal (Post). We can observe the strikingly high similarity for images generated with the same seed (columns), despite using a model retrained from scratch with a considerably smaller subset of the original data.
abstract: Training data attribution (TDA) should enable generative model interpretability and foster a variety of related downstream tasks. Nonetheless, current TDA approaches lack reliability and robustness, preventing their adoption in real-world setups. In this paper, we take a decisive step towards more reliable and robust TDA for diffusion models. We propose to perform TDA with mirrored unlearning and noise-consistent skew (MUCS). The idea is to fine-tune a second model with bounded mirrored gradient ascent, and to measure the normalized skew of this model with respect to the original one using consistent noise samples. We show that, while being conceptually simple and generic, MUCS systematically outperforms existing methods on three different datasets by a large margin. We additionally study the effect that core design choices have on final performance, and analyze novel aspects regarding the overlap of influential instances across generated items and the potential of ensembling TDA approaches. We believe that our findings may have broader implications for more general unlearning setups, as well as for tasks requiring the comparison of diffusion losses.
